stimulus.source_note: Election returns as published by the Library of Congress, Presidential Election of 1860: A Resource Guide (guides.loc.gov/presidential-election-1860), and the American Presidency Project (presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/elections/1860). Popular-vote totals differ slightly between sources because of fusion tickets in New York and New Jersey.
stimulus.text:
Results of the presidential election of November 6, 1860. The Electoral College had 303 votes; 152 were needed to win.

| Candidate | Party | Popular votes | Share | Electoral votes |
| Abraham Lincoln | Republican | 1,865,908 | 39.8% | 180 |
| Stephen A. Douglas | Democratic | 1,380,202 | 29.5% | 12 |
| John C. Breckinridge | Southern Democratic | 848,019 | 18.1% | 72 |
| John Bell | Constitutional Union | 590,901 | 12.6% | 39 |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to the table, which candidate won the most electoral votes while winning less than 40 percent of the popular vote?

options.misconception: Background: Douglas came second in the popular vote, but the table gives him only 12 electoral votes.
Background: Breckinridge won 72 electoral votes, well short of Lincoln's 180.
Background: Bell won 39 electoral votes, fewer than Breckinridge and far fewer than Lincoln.

rationales.A: Background: Douglas came second in the popular vote, but the table gives him only 12 electoral votes.
rationales.B: Lincoln's row shows 180 electoral votes and 39.8 percent of the popular vote — the most electoral votes, and under 40 percent.
rationales.C: Background: Breckinridge won 72 electoral votes, well short of Lincoln's 180.
rationales.D: Background: Bell won 39 electoral votes, fewer than Breckinridge and far fewer than Lincoln.
rationales.general:
1. Read Lincoln's row across: 180 electoral votes, 39.8 percent of the popular vote.
2. Check the others: no one else tops 72 electoral votes.
3. Background: Lincoln won because his votes were packed in the populous North, where the Electoral College gave him whole states at once.
4. So a candidate can sweep the Electoral College without winning a majority of the people.
Remember: electoral votes are won state by state, so a regional sweep can beat a national plurality.
